## eDNA QA/QC steps

In the specific case of eDNA, data stream 2 would require a carefully considered sampling and analysis pipeline. First, sequence reads are processed to resolve unique amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) and quantify the reads associated with each ASV. Second, ASVs are taxonomically classified using reference databases. Third, these taxonomic assignments are used to group ASVs into the sampled target source groups. In blue carbon research, for example, these groups represent primary producers capable of fixing organic carbon through photosynthesis (e.g. mangroves, seagrass [@reef2017aslo; @ortega2020aslo; @erlania2023scitot]). ASVs that cannot be assigned confidently to a characterised source category may provide evidence of unresolved compositional mass. Their inclusion in the pooled unsampled category requires explicit filtering and justification because taxonomic non-assignment may also arise from incomplete reference databases, sequence quality, off-target amplification or classification uncertainty (Fig. S8). Therefore, the success of this strategy depends on some key assumptions regarding the relative detectability of different source groups, which is linked in some part to relative rates of shedding and decay, along with primer choices, amplification efficiencies, and sequencing bias [@beng2020biodiv]. Consequently, observed read proportions need not scale with biomass, dietary contribution or carbon contribution among source groups. Further experimental work is needed to quantify how taxon-specific shedding, degradation, extraction, marker-copy variation, primer affinity and amplification affect relationships among sequence-read proportions, biomass and carbon contribution.
